policies.M156:c08: Publish what was done to the animals and what the study found, so that the harm and its justification can be judged outside the review committee, including studies that produced no usable result.
policies.M157:c01: Permit primate work only where the model is scientifically necessary and no valid alternative can answer the question, under enhanced welfare review, with each element established independently and recorded.
policies.M157:c02: Prohibit significant-harm primate research even where scientifically useful, on the ground that cognitive capacities impose a higher bar, with the prohibition defined by severity rather than by species alone.
policies.M157:c03: Permit only low or moderate severity, with exceptions confined to life-saving objectives defined in advance and approved by a body outside the institution.
policies.M157:c04: Phase out primate use as alternatives mature, with explicit replacement milestones, dates, and public reporting of progress against them.
policies.M157:c05: Permit case-by-case use with a strong harm-benefit justification, with the justification specific to the study rather than to the research programme, and reassessed on renewal.
policies.M157:c06: Reject instrumental harmful use of great apes and highly cognitively complex primates, with the covered species listed and the list revised as evidence about cognition develops.
policies.M157:c07: Require independent species-specific ethics review with public reporting, conducted by reviewers with relevant expertise and their decisions published in summary.
policies.M157:c08: Require public reporting of severity and outcomes for every primate study, so that the case for continuing this work rests on what it has produced rather than on what it promised.
policies.M158:c01: Approve the severe challenge only where it is scientifically necessary and humane endpoints and minimisation are optimised, with the endpoints defined before approval and their application audited.
policies.M158:c02: Require a lower-severity design even at reduced information yield where severe morbidity is not indispensable, with indispensability argued rather than asserted.
policies.M158:c03: Reject any study above an absolute welfare ceiling regardless of scientific value, with the ceiling stated in the institution's policy rather than judged per protocol.
policies.M158:c04: Run a staged pilot to establish whether a lower challenge severity can answer the question, with escalation permitted only on the pilot's result and reviewed before it proceeds.
policies.M158:c05: Weigh expected benefit against harm under a stated framework, with both quantified as far as possible and the assessment recorded for later comparison with what the study delivered.
policies.M158:c06: Reject severe challenge on anti-instrumentalisation grounds, with the position stated as a limit on what may be done rather than as a factor to weigh.
policies.M158:c07: Require non-animal and in vitro evidence to exhaust the reducible uncertainty before any severe challenge, with that evidence presented in the protocol.
policies.M158:c08: Publish the severity endpoints in advance and report what actually happened, so that the promised limits can be checked afterwards, including where endpoints were exceeded.
policies.M159:c01: Meet regulatory research-animal welfare minimums with veterinary care and committee oversight, with compliance documented and inspections recorded.
policies.M159:c02: Require enhanced species-specific welfare beyond ordinary laboratory minimums, on the ground that these animals are bred, live and are killed as organ sources, with the standards written and audited.
policies.M159:c03: Prohibit programme configurations that cause chronic severe welfare impairment even where they improve biosecurity, with the prohibited configurations named rather than assessed case by case.
policies.M159:c04: Provide housing, social contact and behavioural opportunity to the maximum compatible with pathogen control, with the trade-off documented for each restriction rather than assumed.
policies.M159:c05: Permit source-animal use for major human benefit under stringent welfare conditions, with those conditions specified, monitored and reported alongside transplant outcomes.
policies.M159:c06: Reject breeding and killing sentient animals as organ inventories, with the position stated as a limit on the programme rather than as a welfare standard within it.
policies.M159:c07: Require independent welfare audit, public reporting and refinement benchmarks, with the benchmarks improving over time and progress against them published.
policies.M159:c08: Require independent inspection with published findings, so that welfare inside a closed facility can be verified rather than asserted, including unannounced inspections.
policies.M160:c01: Prohibit medically important antimicrobials for growth promotion and for routine prevention without diagnosed disease, with the prohibition enforced through prescribing rules and monitored through sales data.
policies.M160:c02: Permit therapeutic treatment of clinically ill animals under veterinary oversight, with diagnosis recorded and treatment limited to the affected animals and the necessary course.
policies.M160:c03: Permit narrowly defined group prevention in high-risk groups where husbandry alternatives are insufficient, with the definition written, time-limited and reviewed against use data.
policies.M160:c04: Ban preventive use more strictly and require husbandry and biosecurity instead, with the transition period stated and the husbandry standards specified.
policies.M160:c05: Oppose restrictions that would leave sick animals untreated, on welfare grounds, with the concern addressed through diagnosis-based access rather than by relaxing the prohibition.
policies.M160:c06: Prioritise preserving antimicrobial effectiveness under a One Health standard, with the reduction targets stated, monitored and reported across sectors.
policies.M160:c07: Couple restrictions with husbandry investment so that costs do not drive under-treatment, with the support funded and its uptake reported alongside use data.
policies.M160:c08: Publish farm-level antimicrobial use so that buyers and the public can see what a producer actually uses, with the data comparable across producers rather than self-described.
policies.M161:c01: Cull rapidly on infected premises with movement control, surveillance and biosecurity, with the criteria for culling defined in advance and the perimeter set by risk assessment.
policies.M161:c02: Use vaccination as a complementary control where risk analysis supports it, with the analysis published and the vaccination programme monitored for effect on transmission.
policies.M161:c03: Use targeted ring vaccination with limited culling, with the ring size set by risk assessment and both interventions reported afterwards.
policies.M161:c04: Vaccinate preventively in high-risk regions before outbreak expansion, with the regions identified on stated criteria and the programme reviewed against subsequent outbreaks.
policies.M161:c05: Minimise killing while controlling transmission, on welfare grounds, with the number of animals killed reported and alternatives documented for each decision.
policies.M161:c06: Choose the fastest reliable eradication strategy on public and animal health grounds, with reliability assessed on evidence and the choice explained rather than defaulted to.
policies.M161:c07: Escalate from surveillance and biosecurity through vaccination to culling according to outbreak risk and vaccine constraints, with the escalation criteria published in advance.
policies.M161:c08: Compensate affected farmers promptly and in full, so that reporting an outbreak does not ruin the household that reports it, with payment timelines stated and met.
policies.M162:c01: Use targeted lethal control where necessary for major ecological benefit, with humane methods specified, operators trained, and welfare outcomes monitored and reported.
policies.M162:c02: Use fertility control or other non-lethal management where it is effective, with effectiveness assessed against the ecological objective and the method reviewed as evidence accumulates.
policies.M162:c03: Use exclusion and habitat modification before any direct killing, with those measures implemented and their results assessed before lethal control is considered.
policies.M162:c04: Do not intervene where the harms of control exceed the ecological benefit or where repeated killing cannot achieve the objective, with both assessed in advance and revisited.
policies.M162:c05: Favour effective population reduction on conservation grounds, with the ecological objective stated numerically and progress toward it reported.
policies.M162:c06: Oppose lethal control where less harmful options exist, with those options identified specifically and their feasibility assessed rather than dismissed on cost alone.
policies.M162:c07: Manage adaptively with welfare monitoring and stop-and-review criteria set in advance, with the programme paused when those criteria are met rather than continued to completion.
policies.M162:c08: Decide with the island community and publish the method chosen, so that people living with the outcome chose it, and report back on what it achieved.
policies.M163:c01: Vaccinate or otherwise intervene where the disease threatens public health or conservation and the intervention is effective, with effectiveness established and the programme monitored.
policies.M163:c02: Intervene specifically to reduce severe wild-animal suffering where ecological risk is low, with the suffering documented and the ecological assessment made in advance.
policies.M163:c03: Do not intervene where the ecological effects of manipulation are too uncertain, naming the uncertainty and what evidence would resolve it so the position can change.
policies.M163:c04: Intervene in high-burden populations with monitoring rather than running an ecosystem-wide programme, with the boundary of the intervention stated and its effects tracked.
policies.M163:c05: Favour reducing preventable suffering on welfare grounds, with the scale of suffering estimated and the intervention's expected effect on it stated.
policies.M163:c06: Favour restraint on grounds of ecological integrity and wildness, with the value being protected articulated rather than assumed, and exceptions defined narrowly.
policies.M163:c07: Integrate animal welfare, ecosystem effects and human disease risk under a One Health rule, with all three assessed and the trade-offs recorded.
policies.M163:c08: Publish the intervention plan and its results, so that people living alongside the population can see what is being done and why, including where it did not work.
policies.M164:c01: Procure plant-forward with reduced animal products, with the reduction expressed as a purchasing target, phased, and reported against.
policies.M164:c02: Require higher-welfare certified animal products wherever animal products are purchased, with the certification named and supplier compliance audited.
policies.M164:c03: Procure the lowest-cost nutritionally adequate menu, stating that welfare and emissions are not among the criteria so the omission is visible rather than implicit.
policies.M164:c04: Set a greenhouse-gas or sustainability threshold for vendors, with the threshold stated in tender documents and compliance verified rather than self-declared.
policies.M164:c05: Preserve animal-product availability for patient and cultural choice while shifting defaults, with the alternatives always available and no additional cost or delay attached.
policies.M164:c06: Reduce demand for intensive-production products on animal-welfare grounds, with the production systems being avoided defined and the shift measured in purchasing.
policies.M164:c07: Prioritise lower-emission menus while protecting nutrition and access, with nutritional adequacy assessed for the populations served and access monitored after any change.
policies.M165:c01: Choose the lower-carbon option wherever clinical quality and safety are preserved, with that judgment made against stated clinical criteria and recorded in the procurement decision.
policies.M165:c02: Apply a proportional carbon requirement using a stated marginal cost per tonne threshold, published so that decisions can be checked against it rather than justified afterwards.
policies.M165:c03: Prioritise direct clinical capacity and make decarbonisation voluntary where budgets are severely constrained, with the constraint stated and the position reviewed as budgets change.
policies.M165:c04: Set lifecycle procurement and carbon targets with supplier accountability, with the targets written into contracts and supplier performance reported publicly.
policies.M165:c05: Treat decarbonisation as a health duty because healthcare emissions cause health harm, with that harm quantified for the system's own emissions rather than argued in general.
policies.M165:c06: Require any climate spending to justify the health services it displaces, with the comparison made explicitly and published rather than left as an implicit trade-off.
policies.M165:c07: Publish the health system's emissions and its reduction plan, so that patients and staff can hold it to what it has said, with progress reported annually against the plan.
policies.M166:c01: Allocate to maximise expected health loss averted, with the estimates and their assumptions published and revisited as adaptation projects report outcomes.
policies.M166:c02: Prioritise the most climate-vulnerable and worst-off populations, with vulnerability measured on stated indicators and the resulting allocation published.
policies.M166:c03: Set geographic minimum floors so that smaller regions are not abandoned, with the floors fixed before allocation and protected from reallocation.
policies.M166:c04: Protect critical health-system infrastructure first, with the assets classified as critical listed in advance rather than identified after an event.
policies.M166:c05: Combine vulnerability, health gain, feasibility and equity under a published rule stating how much each contributes, applied consistently across rounds.
policies.M166:c06: Prioritise the worst-off on climate-justice grounds, with the comparison made on stated measures and the allocation reported against them.
policies.M166:c07: Favour scalable interventions with high benefit across scenarios, with the scenarios stated and robustness reported rather than a single central estimate.
policies.M166:c08: Give the communities most exposed a standing role in setting priorities, and publish where the money went, with the role continuing between funding rounds rather than convened for each.
policies.M167:c01: Prioritise those at highest medical risk from heat, using stated clinical criteria — age, cardiorespiratory and renal conditions, medications — identified from existing records rather than at the door.
policies.M167:c02: Prioritise people who lack cooling at home or the transport to reach it, identified through stated indicators rather than self-report at the point of need, and reached actively during the heatwave.
policies.M167:c03: Open access first-come while reserving a stated quota for high-risk people, held back until a defined point in the day so that the quota is not exhausted by early arrivals.
policies.M167:c04: Deploy resources geographically to the hottest and highest-risk neighbourhoods, using measured temperature and vulnerability data rather than existing service locations, and publish the map.
policies.M167:c05: Allocate to reduce expected harm, using stated risk estimates, and report afterwards what the deployment is estimated to have prevented so the rule can be revised.
policies.M167:c06: Give priority to the worst-off, with disadvantage assessed on stated indicators rather than inferred from who presents, and the priority applied at the point of deployment rather than at the door.
policies.M167:c07: Where the resources cannot distinguish further among similarly high-risk eligible people, allocate by lottery, run openly, with the eligibility criteria published beforehand.
policies.M168:c01: Give equal continuity of essential and chronic care irrespective of displacement or migration status, with the entitlement effective on arrival and not conditional on registration that takes weeks.
policies.M168:c02: Provide portable coverage, records and medication entitlement for the period of displacement, with a defined duration, a route to renew it, and records transferable without the person having to obtain them.
policies.M168:c03: Under severe host scarcity, provide a staged package prioritising emergency and essential services, with the stages defined in advance and the same package applying to hosts and displaced people alike.
policies.M168:c04: Allocate to hosts and displaced people under one vulnerability-based rule rather than two systems, with the rule published and its application reported by group so that neither is quietly disadvantaged.
policies.M168:c05: Include on equal-status grounds, treating exclusion as a wrong independent of its consequences, with any limit justified in the same terms that would be used for residents.
policies.M168:c06: Permit transparent limits on service priority under scarcity while rejecting a categorical host-first rule, with the limits stated as clinical categories and reviewed as capacity changes.
policies.M168:c07: Give displaced people the same access as residents from the day they arrive, and carry their records with them, with the transfer arranged by the services rather than left to the person.
policies.M169:c01: Permit tightly limited outdoor research under independent governance and environmental assessment, with the scale, materials and duration fixed in the authorisation and monitoring reported publicly.
policies.M169:c02: Confine work to laboratory and modelling until international governance is stronger, naming what would count as sufficient governance so that the restriction has an end condition.
policies.M169:c03: Require consent or consultation from the communities at any experimental site, obtained before the work is designed rather than after, with the outcome published and binding on the decision.
policies.M169:c04: Hold a moratorium on field experiments that release substances, defined by what is released rather than by intent, and reviewed on a stated schedule against named evidence gaps.
policies.M169:c05: Favour generating knowledge before a climate emergency narrows the options, with the research bounded by scale and risk ceilings and its results placed in the public domain.
policies.M169:c06: Oppose unilateral field experimentation on precautionary and governance grounds, requiring international authorisation before any outdoor work regardless of scale.
policies.M169:c07: Require registration in an international registry with predefined scale and risk ceilings, transparent protocols, and results published whether or not the experiment succeeds.
policies.M170:c01: Move from contained testing to field testing in defined stages under a risk-and-benefit framework, with the criteria for each stage set in advance and independent confirmation before moving on.
policies.M170:c02: Release in the field only after meaningful community engagement and after regulatory and ecological thresholds are met, with engagement judged by what was changed as a result rather than by attendance.
policies.M170:c03: Keep trials contained until longer-term ecological evidence is stronger, naming the evidence sought and the monitoring that would produce it so the restriction can end.
policies.M170:c04: Require authorisation from the local community before any release affecting the shared environment, exercised through a body the community recognises, and revocable before release.
policies.M170:c05: Favour deployment where disease burden is high and expected benefit substantial, with both stated numerically and monitoring in place to confirm the benefit materialises.
policies.M170:c06: Favour reversible and localised strategies on ecological precautionary grounds, with reversibility defined operationally — what could be stopped, how quickly, and by whom.
policies.M170:c07: Release adaptively under independent monitoring with stop criteria fixed in advance and data published as it is collected, so that a decision to continue is made on visible evidence.
policies.M170:c08: Require the consent of the communities where release would occur, obtained before trials begin and revocable up to release, with the outcome of the consent process published.
policies.M171:c01: Maximise total health gain regardless of borders, applying one cost-effectiveness standard to domestic and international spending and publishing what each pound bought in each.
policies.M171:c02: Give special weight to residents, with the weight stated as a factor rather than left implicit, so that the size of the partiality is visible and can be argued about.
policies.M171:c03: Prioritise populations abroad who are much worse off, with the comparison made on stated measures and the resulting allocation published alongside domestic spending.
policies.M171:c04: Set a fixed floor for international assistance and allocate the remainder domestically, with the floor protected from in-year reallocation and reported against annually.
policies.M171:c05: Allow bounded national partiality on reciprocity and community grounds, with the bound expressed as a floor for assistance below which partiality may not go.
policies.M171:c06: Apply cost-effectiveness with equity weights for global poverty and burden, publishing the weights so that the trade-off between efficiency and equity is inspectable.
policies.M171:c07: Tie the aid share to a transparent public authorisation while preserving a humanitarian minimum that no mandate can reduce, with both the mandate and the minimum stated.
policies.M171:c08: Decide the domestic and international split through public deliberation and publish the reasoning, so that the balance is a stated choice rather than a residual. The deliberation happens before the budget is set, its participants and terms are published, and the split is revisited on a fixed schedule rather than only when it is challenged.
policies.M172:c01: Maximise total expected health gain, applying the rule to identifiable and statistical patients alike and recording what the identifiable patient's claim would have cost.
policies.M172:c02: Rescue the identifiable person where death or major harm is imminent, despite lower aggregate gain, with imminence defined in advance and the aggregate cost stated when the decision is made.
policies.M172:c03: Give priority by severity and to the worst-off, bounded by a cost-effectiveness threshold, with both the severity measure and the bound published so that the limit of the priority is known.
policies.M172:c04: Where the moral claims are close, decide by lottery between rescue and the population programme, with closeness defined on stated criteria and the draw conducted openly.
policies.M172:c05: Apply an age or lifetime modifier only where it can be justified independently of who is identifiable, stating that justification, and never as a proxy for salience.
policies.M172:c06: Balance gain, severity, urgency and budget impact under a published rule that says how much each contributes, applied by a standing body rather than case by case.
policies.M172:c07: Reject salience as a legitimate allocation factor while allowing severity to count, with the distinction applied by asking whether the same claim would be honoured for an unidentified patient.
policies.M172:c08: Apply a published institutional rule deciding rescue-versus-programme cases in advance, and require committee review of any departure from it, with departures reported.
policies.M173:c01: Guarantee post-trial access to the beneficial intervention for participants who still need it, for a stated duration, funded and arranged before enrolment opens.
policies.M173:c02: Negotiate broader community health-system and capacity benefits rather than product access alone, with the benefits identified by the community and written into the agreement.
policies.M173:c03: Provide both participant post-trial access and a community infrastructure and training plan, with each specified separately so that one cannot substitute for the other.
policies.M173:c04: Let community engagement determine the locally valued benefit package within stated ethical minimums, with those minimums non-negotiable and the rest genuinely open.
policies.M173:c05: Require that communities share in the value the research generates, with the mechanism named and its delivery reported after the trial ends rather than promised during recruitment.
policies.M173:c06: Allow diverse non-product benefits where they are responsive to what the community identified and sustainable after the trial, with sustainability assessed against who will fund them afterwards.
policies.M173:c07: Prohibit benefit arrangements large enough to distort consent or community authorisation, or to substitute for fair baseline conditions, with the limit assessed by an independent committee.
policies.M174:c01: Allocate across impact, vulnerability and need, country ownership and efficiency under a published multiprinciple rule, with the weight of each stated and the resulting allocation reported.
policies.M174:c02: Maximise expected climate and health impact per unit of finance, publishing the estimates used and revisiting them as projects report outcomes.
policies.M174:c03: Reserve a floor for least-developed countries, small island states and the most vulnerable, ring-fenced from competitive allocation and disbursed on the same timetable.
policies.M174:c04: Allocate per capita or by a published vulnerability index, with the index components and data sources stated so that a country can check its own position.
policies.M174:c05: Weight allocation by historical emissions and capacity to pay, stating the measure of responsibility used and the period it covers.
policies.M174:c06: Require that allocations follow nationally identified priorities rather than donor optimisation alone, with the country's own plan attached to the funding decision.
policies.M174:c07: Balance immediate adaptation and long-term resilience across the portfolio, with the split stated in advance and reported against rather than emerging from project selection.
policies.M174:c08: Let recipient countries set their own adaptation priorities within the allocation, and publish what each received and what it chose, so that ownership is visible rather than asserted.
policies.M175:c01: Present plant-forward options as the default while keeping meat and animal products available on request without extra cost, delay or explanation, with the default set at the menu level rather than by rationing.
policies.M175:c02: Present all options equally with no default, ordering and placement chosen to avoid steering, and the neutrality of the presentation checked rather than assumed.
policies.M175:c03: Set a mandatory procurement target reducing high-impact animal products while preserving individual choice, with the target expressed in purchasing rather than in what any person may eat.
policies.M175:c04: Serve the lowest-cost nutritionally adequate menu without an environmental default, stating that environmental impact is not among the criteria so the omission is visible.
policies.M175:c05: Permit welfare-improving defaults with an easy opt-out, on the ground that some presentation is unavoidable, provided the opt-out is genuinely costless and stated on the menu.
policies.M175:c06: Oppose defaults set without an explicit institutional mandate, on autonomy grounds, requiring any default to be authorised through the institution's own decision process rather than by the caterer.
policies.M175:c07: Consult the people who eat there and publish the result, so that a default is set with them rather than for them, and revisit it on a stated schedule.
